pairs.text: Last week, I tried to teach a CNC lathe in a factory outside Turin to follow a laser pointer.
A camera watches the dot, a laptop does the maths, and the lathe moves its tool to match.
The first test, the tool slammed into the chuck and a puff of smoke rose from the motor driver.
Here is the invisible part. A control loop is just a question asked over and over.
The loop overcorrects, then overcorrects the correction, and the whole thing starts to shake.
My fix was a PID controller.
Proportional pushes toward the target.
Integral remembers the past, derivative predicts the future, and calms everything down.
I also threw away the webcam and wired a sensor straight into a microcontroller.
The new test ran on a robot arm first, because I like my lathe alive.
It tracked the dot across the bench like a very polite cat.
Then back to the lathe.
Just a tool following a light in a factory at night, and me pretending that was always the plan.
A factory outside Turin.
The tool slammed into the chuck of the lathe.
A puff of smoke rose from the motor driver.
A short circuit threw sparks across the circuit board.
The motor driver is an H-bridge made of transistors.
The program crashed with an error on my laptop screen.
I measured the metal part with a gauge.
I repaired the phone on the workbench with tweezers.
A welder in the workshop throws bright sparks.
The city at night, full of lights and traffic.
A close-up of a motherboard full of components.
An abandoned rusty machine in an old factory hall.
I soldered the sensor wires onto the board.
The small hobby robot has servo motors and ultrasonic eyes.
A castle in Turin, Italy.
The camera sends the error back to the controller, which pushes the motor toward the target.
